title: Inheritance of radial variation of wood properties and bending properties in full-sib families of Japanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica D. Don)
content:
Abstract
Japanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica D. Don) is the most widely planted tree species in Japan. Despite this, it is known to be inferior to other species in terms of wood quality, especially Young’s modulus. Therefore, improving the wood quality of Japanese cedar has been recognized as an important issue in tree breeding in Japan. The present study aimed (i) to examine the among-family variation of radial variation in wood properties, (ii) to investigate the relationships between wood properties and bending properties, and (iii) to clarify the inheritance of wood properties and bending properties in the juvenile wood of Japanese cedar trees using 18 full-sib families. In addition, the family variation of load–deflection curves was investigated in two radial positions: the inner and outer wood of juvenile wood. The radial variations of all wood properties were affected by their genetic backgrounds rather than by environmental factors. The microfibril angle mainly affected the modulus of elasticity and Janka plastic modulus, while air-dry density mainly influenced the modulus of rupture and bending work. The narrow-sense heritability of almost all properties in inner wood was higher than that of outer wood and ranged from 0.125 for annual ring width to 0.644 for air-dry density. The 18 families were grouped into four and two groups by differences in the types of load–deflection curves in the inner and outer wood, respectively. The commonality of mating parents in families classified in each group and breeding values suggested that differences in load–deflection curves, such as the proportional limit and amount of deflection in the plastic region, were genetically controlled.
